A ball’s chance of being struck depends on the position where it first appears on the three-slot platform:
• start in slot 1 → struck with probability 1⁄3
• start in slot 2 → struck with probability 5⁄9
• start in slot 3 → struck with probability 17⁄27

Every ball after the very first cycle can enter either slot 2 or slot 3, but only ball 3 is guaranteed to begin in slot 3 (ball 1 starts in slot 1, ball 2 in slot 2). Since 17⁄27 ≈ 0.63 is the highest possible striking probability, the optimal choice is the one certain to start in slot 3—ball number 3.
At the instant you must choose, balls 1, 2 and 3 are already on the three-slot platform.  

For a ball now on the platform let  P1 , P2 , P3  be the probabilities it is eventually ejected (and not merely released) when it is currently in slots 1, 2 or 3.

• Slot 1: a piston fires in slot 1 with probability 1⁄3 and ejects the ball; firing in slots 2 or 3 releases it.  
 P1 = 1⁄3.

• Slot 2: with probability 1⁄3 it is itself ejected (piston 2); with probability 2⁄3 it moves to slot 1 (pistons 1 or 3) and thereafter succeeds with probability P1.  
 P2 = 1⁄3 + (2⁄3)P1 = 1⁄3 + (2⁄3)(1⁄3) = 5⁄9.

• Slot 3: with probability 1⁄3 it is ejected (piston 3); with probability 1⁄3 it moves to slot 2 (piston 1) and with probability 1⁄3 it jumps to slot 1 (piston 2).  
 P3 = 1⁄3 + (1⁄3)P2 + (1⁄3)P1 = 1⁄3 + (1⁄3)(5⁄9) + (1⁄3)(1⁄3) = 17⁄27 ≈ 0.6296.

Thus a ball now in slot 3 has the greatest possible chance of being ejected: 17⁄27.

At the moment of choice ball 1 is in slot 1 (chance 1⁄3), ball 2 in slot 2 (5⁄9) and ball 3 in slot 3 (17⁄27). No later ball can exceed the 17⁄27 probability because that is the maximum attainable for any ball in any slot.

Therefore the ball with the highest probability of winning is the one currently numbered 3.

Let H be the number of humans and V the number of vampires, with H+V=100.

Statement each resident makes: “At least one of us is a human.”

1. If H ≥ 1:
   • The statement is true.
   • Humans (truth-tellers) could say it.
   • Vampires (liars) must say something false, so they could not utter this true statement.
   • Yet every resident, including vampires, did utter it. Contradiction. Therefore H ≠ 1,…,100.

2. If H = 0 (so V = 100):
   • The statement “At least one of us is a human” is false.
   • Vampires always lie, so they will all state this false sentence.
   • This matches what you observed.

Thus the only consistent scenario is H = 0 and V = 100.
Each resident says: “At least one of us is a human.”
1. Suppose at least one human exists.
   • The statement is true, so every human could say it.
   • A vampire must lie; it could not repeat a true statement.
   • But all one-hundred residents give the same statement ⇒ impossible.
2. Therefore no humans exist. The statement is false.
   • A false statement is exactly what every vampire would utter.
Hence all one-hundred residents are vampires.

For any such triple, consider Bob’s simultaneous guesses (g,g,g).
He wins g coins from each box that has at least g coins; otherwise he wins 0 from that box.
To maximise the minimum he can guarantee, choose g so that in every triple at least one box contains ≥ g coins.
The largest such g is 12:
• Every distribution above has at least one box with 12 or more coins (y ≥ 12 when x ≤ 0, or z ≥ 12 otherwise).
• If Bob guessed 13, distribution (10,7,13) would give him 0 because no box reaches 13; hence 13 cannot be guaranteed.
Therefore the optimal strategy is to guess 12 coins for each box, guaranteeing at least 12 coins won.
Each coin is worth $1,000, so the minimum money he can be sure to win is 12 × 1,000 = 12,000.
Let the hidden counts be a,b,c with a+b+c=30.
The rules imply that for some pair the difference is exactly six: without loss of generality take c=b+6, so a+2b=24 and a≥0.

Bob must write three numbers before any box is opened.  Because after shuffling he cannot know which guess will be matched with which box, any unequal set of guesses can be permuted by the worst-case arrangement to give him less, so the safest strategy is to put the same guess g on every box.

If Bob writes g on every box he wins g coins for each box that contains at least g coins.  His guaranteed haul is therefore g·m(g) where m(g) is the minimal possible number of boxes that can have at least g coins, over all legal distributions.

For g>12 we can take the distribution 12,12,6 (difference six between the first two boxes) so m(g)=0 and the guarantee is zero.

Take g=12.  The distribution 2,11,17 satisfies the rules and has only one box with 12 or more coins, so m(12)=1, giving a guaranteed haul of 12 coins.

For any smaller g the distribution 1,7,22 (difference six between the first two boxes) shows that m(g)≤1, yielding a guarantee of at most g<12 coins.

Hence no strategy can guarantee more than 12 coins, and writing 12 on each box achieves this bound.
